Comments on question 4
This question was poorly answered and it proved to be the most challenging question in the entire question paper. The
majority of learners only managed to score in the range of 1 to 3 marks by scoring mostly from the marking points MP1,
MP4 and MP7.

What was interesting is that learners appeared to have tried to answer this question from a theoretical, rather than
a practical perspective. The guidance is clear in the question paper regarding the stated reactants (MgCO3 and
HCl) and other apparatus (electrical balance) provided. Surprisingly, learners went on to describe the experiment
using chemicals which are not listed for example magnesium ribbon, calcium carbonate, sodium thiosulfate etc.
Also, although it was clearly stated that learners are not allowed to measure the volume of CO2 gas released in the
reaction, which was a good guidance so that they focus only on measurement of loss of mass, many learners ignored /
overlooked this and went on to describe in terms of volume of CO2 released.

There is a general impression that the majority of learners were merely describing factors that affect the rates of
reactions in general form theory without contextualising this to the given chemicals, apparatus and additional guidance.
A large number of learners for instance made reference to temperature, surface area, the use of a catalyst, the use of
solutions of different concentrations, which were completely out of context.

     96

3    POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS
In general, there is a need to put a great emphasis on assessment objective C and also to make practical work an
integral part of teaching and learning. There are suggested practical activities at the end of each topic in the syllabus
and it is important to expose learners to practical activities in order to reinforce practical (experimental and investigative)
skills and abilities.

Considering that Paper 3 focuses on Assessment Objective C skills, the manner in which learners responded to the
questions in this paper, to a large extent, demonstrated their lack of exposure to practical experiences. Teachers are
encouraged to use easily accessible and locally available / familiar materials to conduct practical activities in their
classrooms. Annexe A on Page 44 of the syllabus outlines the experimental contexts that guide the assessment objective
C skills. It is necessary to take learners through these contexts as well as the requirements for experimental skills as
these are the guidelines for Paper 3. It should be highlighted that the Annexes in the syllabus are there to provide
additional information to teachers and learners regarding aspects of the subject which cannot be explicitly stated in the
specific objectives in the syllabus. It is therefore important that learners are taken through and informed about these
Annexes plus all other additional information in the syllabus preamble and assessment sections.

In conclusion, although NSSCO Chemistry used to be an integral part of NSSCO Physical Science as a Chemistry
section (together with Physics), it is important to reinforce that when Chemistry became a standalone subject, it became
much more demanding compared to when it was just one of the two sections in the old NSSCO Physical Science
curriculum. This is exemplified by the differences in the specifications of assessment objectives for Paper 3 Chemistry
(Assessment objective C only) as compared to the old Physical Science Paper 3 (Assessment objectives A, B and C).
Thus, the teaching of the NSSCO Chemistry needs to be done in the depth that it deserves and not just exactly the same
way we have been teaching the old NSSCO Physical Science curriculum.

Comments on question 4
The complete range of marks was seen in this planning question. The quality of responses was often
centre-dependent.
At some centres, candidates are getting more and more familiar with this type of question and their performance
continues to improve. Better performing candidates at such centres were able to give well sequenced and logical
descriptions of the investigation, in some instances, they were able to draw clear, well labelled diagrams, and were
able to score up to full marks. Most candidates could make some progress and score in the range of 4 to 6 marks.
At other centres, a significant number of candidates demonstrated that they did not have an idea of what a mortar
and pestle is because they often went off-course by stating that they would put the mortar and pestle in a beaker and
crush it. Other candidates demonstrated limited exposure to chromatography as an experimental technique altogether
by going astray and describing biological tests such as iodine test/ benedict’s test, tests for reducing sugars etc.
In general, other candidates used the wrong method such as fractional distillation or crystallisation. These methods
showed a lack of knowledge and understanding of experimental techniques.
Overall, the most common mark awarded was that of the crushing of the flower petals and the filtration of the mixture.

Comments on question 4
Some excellent and fully correct answers to this quantitative planning question were seen. The quality of responses was
often centre-dependent, with some centres doing exceptionally well.
At some centres, candidates are getting more and more familiar with this type of question and their performance
continues to improve. Better performing candidates at such centres were able to give well sequenced and logical
descriptions of the investigation. In some instances, they were able to draw clear, well labelled diagrams, and were able
to score up to full marks. Most candidates could make some progress and score in the range of 4 to 7 marks.
At other centres, a significant number of candidates demonstrated that they were not familiar with rates (speeds) of
reaction as specified in ANNEXE A: Assessment criteria for Paper 3, Alternative to Practical Paper on Page 44 of the
NSSCO 6117 Chemistry syllabus. This question was based on experimental context 1 (b). A considerable number of
candidates demonstrated that they did not understand the purpose of the A4 piece of paper with a cross marked on it
as one of the materials provided on the list. They often went off-course by stating that they will either put the paper on
the mouth of the conical flask; they will use the paper to plot a graph; or they will put the paper inside the conical flask
to mix it with the contents of the conical flask.
In general, a few candidates seemed to have related the A4 piece of paper with a cross marked on it to paper
chromatography experiments because they gave responses which suggest that the cross on the paper needed to
dissolve in a solvent to separate into different colours; or that a solvent needed to be poured onto the paper. This is
probably because Question 4 of the 2022 Chemistry Paper 3 was based on an investigation on paper chromatography.
Overall, the most common marks awarded were those of pouring the acid and the sodium thiosulfate into the conical
flasks. Candidates are advised that ‘amount’ is not an acceptable term for volume (or mass). A minority of candidates
did not attempt the question.

POSITIVE SUGGESTIONS TO TEACHERS
There is an improvement in the quality of responses by candidates in this cohort. Teachers are encouraged to keep
exposing the candidates to practical experiences as a way to improve the performance in this paper for better.
The emphasis is that the experimental contexts that guide the assessment objective C skills are stipulated as ANNEXE
A on page 44 of the NSSCO 6117 Chemistry syllabus. In addition, there are also suggested practical activities at the end
of each topic in the syllabus, which serve as a guide on the practical experiences to be exposed to candidates. These
should serve as guidelines regarding the expectations of Paper 3.
